title: Japan Air Lines 350
summary: Japan Air Lines Flight 350 crashed into Tokyo Bay during final approach to Haneda Airport after the captain deliberately pushed the aircraft into a dive at very low altitude (164 feet). The captain had experienced auditory hallucinations and a mental health crisis in the hours before the flight. The first officer and flight engineer attempted to recover the aircraft but could not overcome the captain's control inputs. The aircraft impacted the water 510 meters short of runway 33R.
probable_cause: The accident resulted from deliberate descent actions by Captain Katagiri who was experiencing a psychiatric crisis manifested by auditory hallucinations, combined with inadequate medical screening and health management that failed to identify his mental condition before he was permitted to operate the aircraft (p. 151-155)

factors.evidence: Captain Katagiri experienced auditory hallucinations and reported to his mother that 'strange things are happening around me' just before accident flight (p. 123-128)
At 08:44:01, Captain Katagiri disengaged autopilot and pushed yoke forward while pulling power levers to idle and engaging thrust reversers (p. 115-120)
First Officer and Flight Engineer attempted to counter captain's control inputs; flight engineer tried to physically restrain captain (p. 115-120)
Inadequate mental health screening and medical oversight failed to identify captain's psychiatric condition before return to duty (p. 130-140)
Aircraft descended rapidly with control column pushed forward; elevator deflection reached +9 degrees nose-down (p. 115-120)
Aircraft impacted Tokyo Bay 510 meters short of runway 33R with nose-down attitude approximately 8 degrees (p. 120-122)

events.text: Japan Air Lines Flight 350 departed Fukuoka on runway 16 with 174 occupants: 8 crew and 166 passengers, with Captain Katagiri at the controls
Aircraft reached cruise altitude of 29,000 feet and transitioned to cruise flight on airway V-17 heading toward Tokyo
Tokyo Control issued descent clearance from cruise altitude to 16,000 feet, and aircraft began descent at 08:22 from position west of Oshima VORTAC

Aircraft transferred to Tokyo Approach Control which issued vector to heading 040 degrees and aircraft continued descent to 3,000 feet, then descended through 8,000 feet when ordered to turn left to heading 360 degrees
Aircraft cleared for ILS approach to runway 33R; current position reported as 16 nautical miles from outer marker; descent profile appeared normal on FDR with speed around 135 knots at 1,000 feet
At 1,000 feet altitude on approach, first officer called 'One Thousand' and instrument checks were confirmed; autopilot coupled approach continuing with landing gear down and flaps at 50 degrees

First officer called 'Five Hundred' at 500 feet altitude during descent; captain did not respond with mandatory 'Stabilized' callout but appeared to acknowledge with nod; descent rate and speed appeared normal
First officer called 'Approaching Minimum' (decision height callout) at 300 feet; captain responded with 'Check' confirming normal procedure; aircraft at approximately 133 knots airspeed

Radio altitude warning sounded three times at 200 feet altitude; middle marker signal began; flight engineer called 'Two Hundred' and first officer called 'Minimum' indicating decision height reached; captain should have called 'Landing' or 'Go Around'

Captain disengaged autopilot and switched to manual control at 164 feet altitude and 130 knots; immediately afterward captain pushed control yoke forward with force and pulled all power levers to idle, engaging thrust reversers on engines 2 and 3
Flight engineer cried out 'We are low' or 'Power low' noticing engine power decrease; aircraft nose dropped abnormally; middle marker signal ceased as aircraft descended below glide slope

First officer reflexively grabbed control column to pull nose up but found it extremely heavy with captain pushing forward with both hands; GPWS 'Glide Slope' warning activated; elevator deflection reached +9 degrees nose-down

Thrust reversers begin to take effect as engines wind down; first officer continues pulling on control column with maximum force trying to raise nose; airspeed dropped to 126 knots; altitude down to 138 feet
First officer succeeds in pulling elevator to approximately -7 degrees (nose-up) but cannot pull further as captain continues pushing down; first officer shouts 'Captain, please stop!'

Aircraft impacts Tokyo Bay water 510 meters short of runway 33R threshold near approach light 14, with nose-down attitude approximately 8 degrees, right bank approximately 7 degrees, and descent angle approximately 18 degrees; left side impact felt by passengers

recommendations.text: Implement comprehensive psychiatric screening program for all flight crew with particular attention to early identification of psychotic disorders and auditory hallucinations
Establish mandatory mental health certification review process for flight crew involving independent psychiatric evaluation, not just internal company medical department
Require flight crews to report any concerning psychological symptoms or behavioral changes to designated medical personnel, with guarantee of impartial evaluation
Enhance cockpit resource management training with focus on procedures for recognizing and responding to incapacitated captain, including override procedures
Strengthen captain medical certification standards and require regular psychiatric evaluation as part of medical certification renewal

notes: Read sections 2.1 (History of Flight, p. 474-604), 3.2.14 (Mental state analysis, p. 123-128), 3.2.10-3.2.12 (Operations analysis, p. 115-120), 4.2 (Probable cause, p. 151-155)

Added 7 CVR extracts from flight recording transcript
